title: Reading for Pleasure Improves Well-being
paragraphs: In an age of smartphones and endless videos, reading a book purely for fun may seem old-fashioned. However, a new review by researchers in the UK suggests that reading for pleasure may have important benefits for people's mental health and brains at every stage of life.

The review was published in the journal Psychological Medicine in 2026. It was written by Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley of the University of Cambridge, together with Vicki Perrin, the head of a reading charity called The Queen's Reading Room. The authors brought together the results of many earlier studies on reading.

According to the review, reading at any age is associated with better well-being, less stress and greater empathy. For example, one study of more than 10,000 young people in the United States found that those who started reading for pleasure early in life performed better on tests of memory and attention. They also had fewer mental health problems, spent less time looking at screens and slept longer. Brain scans showed that they had larger areas in parts of the brain linked to language and emotional control.

The benefits also seem to continue into adulthood. In one survey of around 2,000 people, 74% said that reading had benefited their mental health. Other research has suggested that reading may help reduce feelings of loneliness.

For older people, reading may help protect the brain. One study of more than 5,000 adults aged 55 and over found that frequently doing mental activities, such as reading and playing chess, was linked to a lower risk of developing problems with thinking and memory.
The authors believe that reading, including joining a book club, could be a cheap and easy way to support mental health.

However, there are some important limitations. Most of the studies in the review were observational, which means they cannot prove that reading itself causes these benefits. As one outside expert, Angelina Sutin of Florida State University, pointed out, it is possible that healthier people are simply more likely to read. In addition, one of the authors leads a reading charity.
Meanwhile, surveys in the UK show that reading for pleasure among children is declining, especially among boys aged 11 to 16.
